text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- International financier Goerge Soros, in a letter published in the newspaper, says that a free market is dangerous, and more worrying for democracy than communism. He says today's capitalism is both economically and politically catastrophic and in this situation people could easily turn to a charismatic leader.

- The Swedish state can in the end get a profitable deal for its stake in bank Nordbanken. The bank's share price has developed so strongly that taxpayers can expect a good return of at least 55 billion crown. This was worked out by the newspaper after taking into account the costs of reconstructing the bank after a financial crisis in 1992.

- The new consortium that has taken over glass maker Orrefors Kosta Boda warns about the loss of up to 150 jobs as it looks at rationalising the company after a year of low sales. Production of the Boda brand will be moved in an attempt to cut costs, the company said.

- Wages in Sweden's industrial sector have increased less than feared in the past few years, according to figures from the Metals union. Wages in Sweden's engineering industry rose about 3.6 percent in the 12 months from November 1995 which meant a wage rise of 9.1 percent over the past two years. The Edin committee, set up the by the government to look at wage levels, had recommended a level of 3.5 percent for year rises.

- A batch of jobs are under threat with 150 jobs in danger at the glass works of luxury glass maker Orrefors kosta Boda while telecoms company Ericsson wants to cut its workforce at Norrkoping by 300.
- Swedish power company Sydkraft has bought a 12.5 percent stake of Hamburg utility HEW at the price of 2.8 billion crowns.

- Truck maker Scania has decided that employees will not in the future use Saabs as company cars. About 300 of Scania's 700 company cars are currently Saabs but when their leases expire, staff must change to a different make. A main reason for Scania's decision is apparently the company's ownership of 50 percent of Volkswagon Svenska AB.

- A Gothenburg-based maritime insurer, the Swedish Club, lost five percent of its customer stocks when hull insurance policies were renewed at the end of 1996. In terms of volumes they lost 900,000 dead weight tonnes, Club president Lars Lindfeldt said. Foreign rivals to the Swedish Club lowered their 1997 premiums by 20-30 percent.

- Swedish forestry company AssiDoman said it has taken full control of Russia's AO Segezhabuprom, a sack paper products company near the Finnish border. Another Swedish forestry firm, SCA Molnlycke, also hopes to make investment in Russia, according to company president Kurth Augustson.
